questions.question: What is JpaRepository and why do you extend it instead of CrudRepository?
questions.title: JpaRepository vs CrudRepository — Why Use JpaRepository
questions.direct_answer: **JpaRepository** is the top of Spring Data's repository hierarchy — it extends **CrudRepository** and **PagingAndSortingRepository** and adds JPA-specific methods (`flush()`, `saveAndFlush()`, `deleteAllInBatch()`). It also returns **`List<T>`** instead of `Iterable<T>`, so service code is cleaner and needs no conversion. Extend `JpaRepository` by default; drop to `CrudRepository` only for a deliberately minimal API surface.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the Spring Data repository hierarchy and the concrete, practical reasons JpaRepository is the production default rather than a vague 'it has more methods'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Extending CrudRepository 'because it's simpler', then converting Iterable to List in every service method and missing flush()/batch operations when they're needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the List-vs-Iterable return type and the JPA-only methods (saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch) as concrete reasons, and note JpaRepository is a strict superset so there's no trade-off

sections.title: Why JpaRepository Is the Default
sections.content:
Spring Data JPA stacks its repository interfaces, and each layer adds capability. **`CrudRepository`** gives basic create, read, update, and delete. **`PagingAndSortingRepository`** adds pagination and sorting. **`JpaRepository`** sits at the top, extending both and adding **JPA-specific methods** like `flush()`, `saveAndFlush()`, and `deleteAllInBatch()`.

**Why it matters:** the most practical difference is the return type. `JpaRepository` returns **`List<T>`**, while `CrudRepository` returns **`Iterable<T>`**. A `List` drops straight into your service and controller layers with no conversion step, and it exposes `size()`, indexing, and streaming directly.

**How to choose:** extend `JpaRepository` by default — it is a strict superset, so you lose nothing. Drop to `CrudRepository` only when you deliberately want a tiny API surface, such as a shared module that should expose a minimal contract.

> **The gotcha:** picking `CrudRepository` because it 'sounds lighter' usually backfires — you end up wrapping `Iterable` into `List` in nearly every method and lose batch helpers like `deleteAllInBatch()` that matter for bulk cleanup.

sections.title: Repository Hierarchy at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Repository|~Marker interface|no methods|just enables Spring Data|the root
blue|CrudRepository|~Basic CRUD|save, findById, delete|returns Iterable<T>|minimal surface
emerald|PagingAndSortingRepository|~Adds paging/sort|findAll(Pageable)|findAll(Sort)|extends CrudRepository
violet|JpaRepository|~Full JPA toolkit|flush, saveAndFlush|deleteAllInBatch, returns List<T>|the production default

sections.title: JpaRepository vs CrudRepository
sections.content:
| Aspect | CrudRepository | JpaRepository |
|---|---|---|
| **Return type** | `Iterable<T>` | `List<T>` (directly usable) |
| **Pagination/sorting** | No | Yes (inherited) |
| **Batch ops** | No | `deleteAllInBatch()`, `saveAll()` |
| **Flush control** | No | `flush()`, `saveAndFlush()` |
| **Best for** | Minimal/library API | Everyday Spring Boot apps |

JpaRepository is a strict superset — it has everything CrudRepository has, plus more.

sections.title: CrudRepository — Iterable Forces Conversion
JpaRepository — List Out of the Box
When to Use Which
sections.content: Use **`JpaRepository`** as the default for nearly every Spring Data JPA repository — you get CRUD, paging, sorting, batch operations, and the convenient `List` return type. Use **`CrudRepository`** only when you deliberately want a tiny API surface (a shared module) or a lightweight contract. **`PagingAndSortingRepository`** is rarely chosen directly. In a typical Spring Boot REST API on PostgreSQL, `JpaRepository` covers ~95% of needs without custom code.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing CrudRepository for 'simplicity'** — you then convert `Iterable` to `List` in every service method, which is more code, not less.
- **Missing the JPA-only helpers** — `saveAndFlush()` and `deleteAllInBatch()` aren't available, so bulk deletes load and delete row by row.
- **Assuming there's a trade-off** — `JpaRepository` is a strict superset; defaulting to it costs nothing at runtime.
- **Forgetting it still generates everything** — you never write an implementation; Spring builds the proxy from the method names.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Hierarchy**: `CrudRepository` → `PagingAndSortingRepository` → `JpaRepository`, each adding features.
- **`List` vs `Iterable`** — `JpaRepository` returns `List<T>`, usable without conversion.
- **JPA-only methods** — `flush()`, `saveAndFlush()`, `deleteAllInBatch()` for control and performance.
- **No implementation needed** — Spring generates it at runtime from method names.
- **Default to JpaRepository** — it's a strict superset; you lose nothing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: JpaRepository is the most complete interface Spring Data gives you for JPA entities. It extends both CrudRepository and PagingAndSortingRepository, so you get basic create, read, update, delete plus pagination and sorting out of the box. The main reason I extend JpaRepository instead of CrudRepository is the return type. JpaRepository returns a List, while CrudRepository returns an Iterable. A List is directly usable in my service and controller layers, so I don't have to write conversion code every time I call findAll. JpaRepository also adds JPA-specific methods. The flush method forces Hibernate to write pending changes to the database immediately, which is handy when I need a generated id for the next step. saveAndFlush combines a save and an immediate flush. And deleteAllInBatch issues a single delete statement instead of loading each entity and deleting it one by one, which is much faster for bulk cleanup. A mistake I see freshers make is extending CrudRepository because it sounds simpler, and then they end up with Iterable everywhere and constant conversion. The thing to understand is that JpaRepository is a strict superset. It has everything CrudRepository has plus more, so in a normal Spring Boot app on PostgreSQL there's no downside to making it the default.

questions.question: What is the difference between findAll() and findAll(Sort) in JpaRepository?
questions.title: findAll() vs findAll(Sort) in JpaRepository
questions.direct_answer: `findAll()` returns rows in **database-dependent order** (often insertion order, but not guaranteed). `findAll(Sort.by("name"))` adds an **`ORDER BY`** clause so the **database** sorts — faster and index-friendly versus loading everything and sorting in Java. Combine with `PageRequest` for paginated, sorted results; use `.descending()` and chained `Sort` for multi-field order.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you push sorting to the database (ORDER BY) instead of loading all rows and sorting in memory, and whether you know how to express multi-field and directional sorts
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling findAll().stream().sorted(...) which loads the whole table into memory and fails to scale once the table grows
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention multi-field sorting, Sort.Direction.DESC, ignoreCase(), combining with PageRequest, and the need for an index on sorted columns

sections.title: Database Sorting vs In-Memory Sorting
sections.content:
**`findAll()`** returns all rows with no defined order — you get whatever the database happens to return. **`findAll(Sort)`** pushes an **`ORDER BY`** into the SQL, so the **database** sorts before sending rows back.

**Why it matters:** that single difference is the reason it scales. The engine uses indexes and optimized sort algorithms, whereas sorting in Java means loading every row into memory first and sorting on the JVM heap.

**How to express it:** the `Sort` object specifies field names, direction (asc/desc), case-handling, and multiple criteria. For large tables, combine sorting with pagination (`PageRequest`) so you load and sort only one page at a time.

> **The gotcha:** if you sort by a column with no index, the database still has to scan and sort the whole table — add an index on any column you regularly sort by.

sections.title: Sorting Options at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|findAll()|~No ORDER BY|DB-dependent order|not guaranteed|use only for tiny/unordered sets
blue|findAll(Sort)|~Adds ORDER BY|DB sorts, index-friendly|scales to large tables|the default for lists
emerald|Multi-field|~Tie-breakers|Sort.by(a).and(Sort.by(b))|ORDER BY a, b|stable ordering
violet|Direction + case|~Control output|Sort.by(...).descending()|ignoreCase() = LOWER()|newest-first, A-Z

sections.title: findAll() vs findAll(Sort)
sections.content:
| Aspect | `findAll()` | `findAll(Sort)` |
|---|---|---|
| **SQL** | `SELECT * FROM t` | `SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY field` |
| **Order** | DB-dependent | Explicit, by your fields |
| **Where sorting happens** | In Java (if at all) | In the database |
| **Memory** | Loads all, sorts in RAM | DB sorts before sending |
| **Scales** | Poorly for large tables | Well, with an index |

Rule of thumb: never load everything and sort in Java.

sections.title: Wrong — Load Everything, Sort in Java
Right — Let the Database Sort
When to Use Each
sections.content: Use **`findAll()`** only when order genuinely doesn't matter or the table is tiny. Use **`findAll(Sort.by(...))`** whenever users see an ordered list (customers A-Z, products by price). Use **chained `Sort`** for tie-breakers, **`Sort.Direction.DESC`** for newest-first feeds, and **`PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)`** for any list that can grow past ~50 items. Never `findAll()` then sort with streams in production.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sorting in Java** — `findAll().stream().sorted(...)` loads the entire table into memory and collapses at scale.
- **Unstable order** — relying on `findAll()` to return insertion order; without `ORDER BY` it isn't guaranteed.
- **No index** — sorting on an unindexed column forces a full scan and sort every call.
- **Forgetting tie-breakers** — single-field sorts can shift page boundaries; chain a second field for stable ordering.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`findAll(Sort)` generates `ORDER BY`** — the database sorts using indexes.
- **Multi-field**: `Sort.by("lastName").and(Sort.by("firstName"))` → `ORDER BY last_name, first_name`.
- **Descending**: `Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "createdAt")` or `.descending()`.
- **Case-insensitive**: `Sort.by("name").ignoreCase()` → `LOWER(name)`.
- **Index sorted columns**, and never load all rows to sort them in Java.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: findAll returns all rows without any defined order, so you get whatever the database happens to give back — usually insertion order, but that's not guaranteed. findAll with a Sort argument adds an order-by clause to the SQL, so the database sorts the rows before sending them. The key difference is where the sorting happens. With findAll and Sort, the database does the work, and it can use indexes and optimized sort algorithms. If instead I call findAll and then sort in Java with streams, I'm loading the entire table into memory and sorting it myself, which breaks down once the table has thousands of rows. For example, findAll with Sort dot by name generates select star from users order by name. For tie-breakers I can chain sorts, like Sort dot by last name dot and Sort dot by first name, which becomes order by last name, then first name. For newest-first I use Sort dot by with direction descending and the field. In production I'd usually combine sorting with pagination using PageRequest dot of, passing page, size, and the sort together, so I only load one page at a time. One thing freshers forget is the index. If I sort by a column with no index, the database has to scan and sort the whole table, so I add an index on any column I sort by. The bottom line is simple. Always let the database sort, never load everything and sort in Java.

Can you accept Sort parameters from a REST request in Spring Boot?

questions.question: How does pagination work with JpaRepository?
questions.title: Pagination with JpaRepository and Pageable
questions.direct_answer: Pass a **`Pageable`** to a repository method: `PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)` (page is **zero-indexed**). It returns a **`Page<T>`** holding the data slice plus metadata (total elements, total pages, hasNext) and runs a **count query**. `Page` becomes **`LIMIT`/`OFFSET`** in SQL. Use **`Slice<T>`** for infinite scroll — it skips the count query.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can paginate large datasets correctly and know Page runs an extra count query while Slice does not
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting pages are zero-indexed, and using Page everywhere when Slice avoids a costly count query on huge tables
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Page vs Slice, capping max page size, passing a stable Sort, and that PageRequest maps to LIMIT/OFFSET

sections.title: Pagination Prevents Memory Overload
sections.content:
With thousands or millions of rows, `findAll()` loads everything and can crash the app. **Pagination** fetches data in **chunks** (pages). Spring Data's **`Pageable`** says which page and how many per page; create it with **`PageRequest.of(page, size)`** where **page numbers start at zero**.

**What you get back:** a **`Page<T>`** wrapping the slice plus metadata — total elements, total pages, current page, and `hasNext()`.

**How it maps to SQL:** Spring emits **`LIMIT`/`OFFSET`** (`PageRequest.of(1, 20)` → `OFFSET 20 LIMIT 20`). `Page` also runs a **count query** for the total — great for "Page 2 of 15" controls, but extra cost on huge tables, where **`Slice`** (no count) fits better.

> **The gotcha:** on a million-row table the count query behind `Page` can take seconds; an infinite-scroll feed doesn't need the total, so reach for `Slice` instead.

sections.title: Pagination at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Pageable|~The request|PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)|page is zero-indexed|describes the slice you want
blue|Page<T>|~Slice + metadata|total elements + pages|runs a count query|for numbered pagination UIs
emerald|Slice<T>|~Slice + hasNext|no count query|cheaper on huge tables|for infinite scroll
violet|SQL|~LIMIT/OFFSET|OFFSET = page * size|LIMIT = size|database does the slicing

sections.title: Paginated, Sorted REST Endpoint
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Page where Slice fits** — on million-row tables the count query can take seconds; infinite-scroll UIs don't need totals, so use `Slice`.
- **Off-by-one pages** — pages are **zero-indexed**; if the frontend sends 1-based numbers, subtract 1.
- **No max page size** — a request for `size=1000000` can overwhelm the DB; cap it (e.g., 100).
- **Forgetting sort** — without a stable `Sort`, page boundaries can shift between requests.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`Pageable`** via `PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)` — **page is zero-indexed**.
- **`Page`** = slice + total count + page count; **`Slice`** = slice + `hasNext` (no count).
- Maps to **`LIMIT`/`OFFSET`** SQL — the database does the slicing.
- **Cap page size** to protect the database from abuse.
- Any custom method can accept `Pageable` and return `Page` or `Slice`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Pagination in JpaRepository works by passing a Pageable object to a repository method. The simplest way is PageRequest dot of with a page number and a page size. Page numbers start at zero, so PageRequest dot of zero comma twenty gives me the first twenty records. The method returns a Page object that wraps the data slice plus metadata like total elements, total pages, and whether there's a next page. Under the hood, Spring turns this into SQL with limit and offset. If I request page two with size twenty, the database sees offset forty, limit twenty. One important detail is that Page runs two queries. The first fetches the slice, and the second counts the total rows so the UI can show something like page two of fifteen. That count query can be slow on very large tables. If I'm building an infinite scroll feed where I don't need the total, I use Slice instead of Page. Slice skips the count query and just tells me if there's a next page. I can add sorting by passing a Sort as the third argument to PageRequest dot of. A couple of gotchas. Pages are zero-indexed, so if the frontend sends one-based page numbers I subtract one. And I always cap the page size, because otherwise someone could ask for a million records and overwhelm the database. So the mental model is simple. Pageable describes the slice, Page gives you totals, and Slice is the lighter option for endless scrolling.

questions.question: What is @Query in Spring Data JPA and when do you use it?
questions.title: @Query Annotation in Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: **`@Query`** lets you write a custom **JPQL** (default) or **native SQL** (`nativeQuery = true`) query when derived method names get too complex. Bind values with **`@Param`**. For UPDATE/DELETE you must add **`@Modifying`** and run inside **`@Transactional`** — and consider `clearAutomatically = true` to avoid stale persistence-context data after a bulk write.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you choose JPQL over native by default and know the @Modifying + @Transactional requirement for writes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for native SQL when JPQL works (losing portability), or omitting @Modifying on UPDATE/DELETE and getting a runtime exception
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @Modifying(clearAutomatically=true) to refresh the persistence context after a bulk update, and DTO projections via JPQL constructor expressions

sections.title: When Method Names Aren't Enough
sections.content:
Spring Data generates queries from method names, but names with four or five conditions stacked together become unreadable. **`@Query`** lets you write the exact query.

**Two flavors:** **JPQL** queries entity objects (`SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.status = :status`) and is **database-portable**; **native SQL** (`nativeQuery = true`) queries tables directly for vendor features (PostgreSQL `ILIKE`, window functions, JSON operators).

**Prefer JPQL** — it's portable and field names are validated at startup. Bind values with **`@Param`** matching `:name` placeholders.

> **The gotcha:** for **UPDATE/DELETE** you must add **`@Modifying`** and run inside **`@Transactional`**, or Spring assumes a SELECT and throws at runtime; add `clearAutomatically = true` so a later read doesn't return stale cached entities.

sections.title: @Query at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|JPQL (default)|~Queries entities|portable across databases|fields validated|use this first
blue|Native SQL|~nativeQuery = true|tables and columns|vendor features (JSONB)|escape hatch only
emerald|@Param|~Named binding|:email in query|@Param("email")|safe, readable
violet|@Modifying|~For writes|UPDATE / DELETE|needs @Transactional|clearAutomatically avoids stale cache

sections.title: Wrong — UPDATE Without @Modifying
Right — @Modifying + @Transactional
JPQL, Native, and Projections
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Native SQL by default** — loses portability and field validation; use JPQL first.
- **Missing `@Modifying`** on UPDATE/DELETE — runtime exception; `@Query` expects SELECT otherwise.
- **No transaction** — even with `@Modifying`, the write needs a `@Transactional` boundary.
- **Stale cache after bulk update** — without `clearAutomatically = true`, the next read may return old cached entities.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JPQL** queries entities/fields and is portable; **native SQL** uses `nativeQuery = true` for vendor features.
- **Bind with `@Param("name")`** matching `:name` in the query.
- **`@Modifying` is required** for UPDATE/DELETE, and they must run in a transaction.
- **`clearAutomatically = true`** clears the persistence context to prevent stale reads.
- Use `@Query` for complex joins/aggregations; keep simple lookups as derived methods.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The Query annotation is what I reach for when a derived method name would get too long or when I need logic Spring Data can't generate. There are two flavors. JPQL queries my entity classes, so I write select o from Order o where o dot status equals a parameter. It's database-portable and the field names are checked at startup. Native SQL is raw SQL, switched on with native query equals true, and I use it when I need a database-specific feature like PostgreSQL's case-insensitive ILIKE or window functions. I prefer JPQL because it's portable and validated. I bind values with named parameters, using a colon name in the query and the Param annotation on the method argument. For update or delete queries there's an important rule. I must add the Modifying annotation, otherwise Spring assumes a select and throws an exception at runtime. On top of that, the modifying query has to run inside a transactional boundary. One subtle thing interviewers like is stale data. After a bulk update, the persistence context can still hold the old entity values, so a later read returns stale data. I fix that with Modifying and clear automatically equals true, which clears the context after the write. So my rule of thumb is simple. Derived names for simple lookups, JPQL with Query for complex joins and aggregations, native SQL only when JPQL genuinely can't express it, and always Modifying plus a transaction for writes.

What is @Modifying and when do you need it?

questions.question: How do you add custom implementation to a Spring Data JPA repository?
questions.title: Custom Repository Implementation in Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: Use the **fragment pattern**: define a custom interface (e.g. `OrderRepositoryCustom`), implement it in a class named with the **`Impl`** suffix (`OrderRepositoryCustomImpl`) that injects `EntityManager`, then have the main repository extend **both** `JpaRepository` and the custom interface. Spring composes them into one proxy. Use it for dynamic Criteria queries or batch logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the fragment/Impl-suffix pattern for logic beyond derived methods and @Query
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Breaking the exact Impl naming convention or trying to add a method body to the repository interface itself
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Impl suffix is configurable (repositoryImplementationPostfix) and that the Criteria API fits dynamic, optional-filter searches

sections.title: Custom Logic Beyond Generated Queries
sections.content:
Sometimes you need logic that doesn't fit a method name or `@Query` — a **dynamic search** with optional filters, a stored-procedure call, or Hibernate's **Criteria API** for type-safe queries. The answer is the **fragment pattern**.

**The three pieces:** you define a custom interface, implement it in a concrete class with full **`EntityManager`** access, and have the main repository extend both `JpaRepository` and your custom interface.

**How Spring wires it:** Spring Data finds the implementation by the **`Impl` suffix** and composes a single proxy that exposes both generated and custom methods on one bean.

> **The gotcha:** the implementation class name must be the interface name plus `Impl` exactly — `OrderRepositoryCustomImpl`, never `...Implementation` — or Spring silently never finds it.

sections.title: Fragment Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Custom interface|~Declares the method|OrderRepositoryCustom|no body here|the contract
blue|Impl class|~Holds the logic|OrderRepositoryCustomImpl|injects EntityManager|exact Impl suffix
emerald|Main repository|~Extends both|JpaRepository + Custom|one proxy at runtime|generated + custom together
violet|Use cases|~When to do this|dynamic Criteria queries|batch / stored procs|3rd-party integration

sections.title: Step-by-Step Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | What to do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Define `OrderRepositoryCustom` with the method signature | The contract for custom logic |
| 2 | Implement `OrderRepositoryCustomImpl` (exact `Impl` suffix), inject `EntityManager` | Spring discovers it by name |
| 3 | `OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>, OrderRepositoryCustom` | Combines both fragments |
| 4 | Call the custom method on the normal repository bean | Spring's proxy routes it |

The `Impl` suffix is configurable via `@EnableJpaRepositories(repositoryImplementationPostfix = "...")`.

sections.title: Dynamic Filter Query with Criteria API
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrong name** — the class must be `<CustomInterface>Impl` exactly; `...Implementation` won't be found.
- **Adding a body to the repository interface** — interfaces can't hold logic; that's what the fragment is for.
- **Injecting the main repository into the Impl** — risks a circular dependency; use `EntityManager`.
- **Reinventing dynamic queries** — for many optional filters, Spring Data **Specifications** or **QueryDSL** may be cleaner than hand-written Criteria.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fragment pattern**: custom interface + `Impl` class + main repo extending both.
- **`Impl` suffix is mandatory** (but configurable via `repositoryImplementationPostfix`).
- **Inject `EntityManager`** with `@PersistenceContext` for full JPA access.
- **Criteria API** is ideal for dynamic, optional-filter searches.
- Spring composes generated + custom methods into **one proxy**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: To add custom implementation to a Spring Data repository I use the fragment pattern, which is three steps. First, I create a custom interface with the method signature, say OrderRepositoryCustom with a method findWithFilters. Second, I implement that interface in a class named OrderRepositoryCustomImpl. The Impl suffix is critical because that's exactly what Spring Data looks for. In the implementation I inject the EntityManager with the PersistenceContext annotation, and that's where the real logic lives, maybe a Criteria API query for a dynamic search, or a stored procedure call. Third, I make the main repository interface extend both JpaRepository and my custom interface. At runtime Spring builds one proxy that combines the generated methods and my custom ones, so I call everything on the same repository bean. The classic use case is a search form where users can apply optional filters. I don't know in advance which filters they'll set, so I build the where clause dynamically with the Criteria builder, adding a predicate only when a filter is present. A couple of gotchas. The implementation class name must match exactly, so OrderRepositoryCustomImpl, not OrderRepositoryCustomImplementation, or Spring won't find it. And I shouldn't inject the main repository into the implementation, because that creates a circular dependency, so I use the EntityManager instead. If I find myself writing lots of these, I'd consider Spring Data Specifications or QueryDSL, which handle dynamic queries more elegantly. And the Impl suffix itself is configurable through the EnableJpaRepositories annotation if a team prefers a different convention.

questions.question: What is @Transactional on a Spring Data JPA repository method?
questions.title: @Transactional on Spring Data JPA Methods
questions.direct_answer: **`@Transactional`** runs a method inside one database transaction — all changes commit together or roll back together. Spring Data repository writes are already transactional; you add `@Transactional` at the **service layer** when several repository calls must be **atomic**. Use **`readOnly = true`** for queries (skips dirty checking). Note: self-invocation within the same class bypasses the proxy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you place transactions at the service layer for atomicity and understand Spring's proxy-based behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting @Transactional on repository interfaces (redundant) or calling a @Transactional method from the same class (proxy bypassed, no transaction)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain readOnly=true skipping dirty checking and that checked exceptions don't roll back by default

sections.title: What @Transactional Does
sections.content:
**`@Transactional`** wraps a method in a transaction — a unit of work that either fully commits or fully rolls back. In Spring Data JPA, **repository write methods are already transactional** (save, delete).

**Where it belongs:** you add `@Transactional` at the **service layer** when multiple repository calls must succeed or fail together — e.g. decrement inventory **and** create an order: both or neither.

**The readOnly optimization:** **`readOnly = true`** optimizes pure reads, because Hibernate skips **dirty checking** when nothing should change.

> **The gotcha:** Spring manages transactions with a proxy, so calling a `@Transactional` method from another method in the **same class** bypasses the proxy and no transaction starts — put the boundary on the public entry point instead.

sections.title: @Transactional at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Where it belongs|~Service layer|orchestrates repos|business atomicity|not on controllers
blue|Default rollback|~RuntimeException|auto rollback|checked = no rollback|use rollbackFor for checked
emerald|readOnly = true|~For queries|skips dirty checking|faster reads|signals intent
violet|Proxy limit|~Self-invocation|same-class call bypasses proxy|no transaction starts|call from another bean

sections.title: Wrong — Self-Invocation Skips the Transaction
Right — Transaction at the Public Entry Point
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`@Transactional` on repository interfaces** — redundant; writes are already transactional. It belongs on service methods.
- **Skipping `readOnly = true`** on read-only services — Hibernate needlessly tracks entities for changes.
- **Self-invocation** — calling a `@Transactional` method from another method in the **same class** bypasses the proxy, so no transaction starts.
- **Expecting checked exceptions to roll back** — only `RuntimeException`/`Error` roll back by default; use `rollbackFor = Exception.class` for checked ones.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Repository writes are transactional by default**; put business transactions on **service** methods.
- **Atomicity** — multiple repo calls in one `@Transactional` commit/roll back together.
- **`readOnly = true`** skips dirty checking for faster reads.
- **Default rollback** is on `RuntimeException`; checked exceptions need `rollbackFor`.
- **Proxy limitation** — same-class self-invocation doesn't start a transaction.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The Transactional annotation tells Spring to wrap a method in a database transaction, so either all the changes commit or they all roll back. The important context is that Spring Data repository write methods, like save and delete, are already transactional by default, so I don't put the annotation on repositories. I put it on service methods when several repository calls need to act as one atomic unit. The classic example is checkout. I decrement inventory and create an order, and both must succeed together. If decrementing stock throws, Spring rolls back the order creation automatically. For read-only service methods I use Transactional with read only equals true. That tells Hibernate to skip dirty checking, because nothing should change, and it speeds reads up. A subtle trap is self-invocation. Spring manages transactions with a proxy, and if one method calls another Transactional method in the same class directly, the call doesn't go through the proxy, so no transaction starts. The fix is to put the boundary on the public entry point, or call across beans. Another gotcha is rollback rules. By default only runtime exceptions trigger a rollback, so if I throw a checked exception I need rollback for equals Exception dot class. The key insight is that transactions are a service-layer, business-logic concern, not a repository detail.
